It seems somewhat unique. If I book a $400/night hotel room, I'll probably get a champagne upon checking in, and maybe a drink coupon, but there's no open bar. In terms of luxury travel, the only situations I can think of when I'm invited to drink all I want is (1) the first/business class air ticket, (2) a wedding.

I would think airlines would have thought, back in the 50s when this became a thing, to try to charge the first class passenger per-drink. They can afford it, and that's the attitude a 4-5 star hotel takes with the minibar.

So, Voat, how do you all think this got started? I tried googling around but didn't really find any definitive answer.
What are the origins of the open bar in first class air cabins? Before planes, did first class train cabins get an open bar?

I don't know. However, when I was a child, I remember during flights there was a drinks menu and you could order whatever you wanted whenever you wanted, irrespective of seating class. The only difference between classes, was what was on the menu; but even in economy there were basic spirits, wine, and beer. In my experience, it's only been a recent trend (the last 10-15 years) to start cashing in on customers by taking money in-flight (possibly as a result of budget airlines springing up).

For what it's worth, there are many occasions with open bars in my experience. Cruise ships tend to have drinks packages, all corporate gatherings are open bar, wakes are open bar, etc. Unless you're impoverished, though, an open bar really doesn't mean much.

Hmmm. That was probably the case when I was a child too, but I didn't fly much until my mid-late twenties. Never been on a cruise.

I agree with all you said. But unlike wakes, or corporate gatherings, airfare is purely commercial. It just strikes me as unusual that airlines said, at some point, let's not bother charging for drinks. I can't think of a single commercial similarity like that. Seems like a strange business decision, and maybe even a liability in this day and age.

My guess (and it's definitely only a guess) is that it was one of two things. Either airfares initially were so expensive relative to the cost of drinks that it wasn't worth charging for the drinks or felt crass to do so. Or, airline competition caused someone to offer it in an attempt to win customers, and other airlines then matched them.

On European airlines it varies from airline to airline whether you pay or not. Fly with EasyJet or RyanAir and you'll pay for water, fly with KLM or BA or whoever and you can have beer or wine for free. It's one of the main differences between flying economy with the cheap or more expensive airlines along with whether or not you get hand luggage only or a hold bag too.
